title: Review: لَيْسَ and Its خَبَر, Numbers 11–20, اسْم التَّفْضِيل, and Answering a Negative Question with بَلَى
summary: A revision session ahead of the test, covering the full chart of لَيْسَ and the two ways its خَبَر may appear — with a fatḥa, or preceded by the بَاء — each illustrated from the Qur'ān. The class then rebuilds the rules for numbers eleven to twenty, where the counted noun always takes a fatḥa but the gender agreement flips between 11–12 and 13–19, and finishes with اسْم التَّفْضِيل on the pattern أَفْعَل, which means more when followed by مِن and most when made مُضَاف.
key_points: لَيْسَ is a word of negation that is not strictly a verb but conjugates on the pattern of the مَاضِي, changing with person, number and gender: لَسْتُ (I am not), لَيْسَ (he is not), لَيْسَتْ (she is not), لَيْسُوا (they m. are not), لَسْنَ (they f. are not).

The خَبَر of لَيْسَ can be handled two ways with no difference in meaning: it takes a fatḥa — لَيْسَ الطَّالِبُ جَدِيدًا — or it is preceded by the بَاء, a حَرْف الجَرّ, which gives it a kasra: لَسْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِمُسَيْطِرٍ.
Numbers 11 to 20 always put the مَعْدُود (maʿdūd : the thing counted) in the accusative with a fatḥa, and in the singular.
For 11 and 12 the عَدَد (ʿadad : the number) matches the gender of the مَعْدُود — أَحَدَ عَشَرَ طَالِبًا against إِحْدَى عَشْرَةَ طَالِبَةً — and every part carries a fatḥa.
For 13 to 19 the rule splits: the first part of the number takes the opposite gender to the مَعْدُود while عَشَر takes the same gender — ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ طَالِبًا against ثَلَاثَ عَشْرَةَ طَالِبَةً.
مِائَة and أَلْف take their counted noun in the singular, and their own form does not change for gender.
اسْم التَّفْضِيل (ism al-tafḍīl) is formed on the pattern أَفْعَل: جَمِيل gives أَجْمَل, كَبِير gives أَكْبَر, نَحِيف gives أَنْحَف, وَاسِع gives أَوْسَع, فَصِيح gives أَفْصَح.

Followed by مِن it is comparative — أَطْوَلُ مِنْهُ (taller than him); made مُضَاف to what follows it is superlative — أَطْوَلُ طَالِبٍ فِي الْفَصْلِ (the tallest student in the class). Context alone decides which.
اسْم التَّفْضِيل is غَيْر مُنْصَرِف (ghayr munṣarif : diptote) and never carries tanwīn.
أَحْمَد is itself an اسْم التَّفْضِيل from حَمْد (praise), meaning the most praised, while مُحَمَّد means the intensely praised one.

Answering a negative question needs care: to أَلَسْتُ أَحْسَنَ طَالِبٍ فِي الْفَصْلِ, replying نَعَمْ confirms the negative — yes, you are not. To affirm, the answer is بَلَى, which negates the negation.
In a name, ابْن takes the same vowel as the word before it, being its صِفَة, while being مُضَاف to the word after it, which therefore takes a kasra: خَالِدُ بْنُ الْوَلِيدِ.

جَمْع مُذَكَّر سَالِم (jamʿ mudhakkar sālim : sound masculine plural) shows case by letter rather than vowel — a wāw for the nominative, مُسْلِمُونَ, and a yāʾ for the accusative and genitive, مُسْلِمِينَ — as distinct from جَمْع تَكْسِير (broken plural).

The ordinals are الْأَوَّل، الثَّانِي، الثَّالِث، الرَّابِع، الْخَامِس، السَّادِس، السَّابِع، الثَّامِن، التَّاسِع، الْعَاشِر, and they have feminine forms too. Unlike plain counting, they express order.
أَخِي الشَّقِيق means my full blood brother; the word شَقِيق rules out the loose use of أَخِي that Arabs apply to anyone.

مَنِ الْأَخ is a courteous way of asking who are you, sidestepping the bluntness of the direct second person — comparable to the South Asian and South African habit of addressing an elder in the third person.
questions: [00:06:02] Q: What happens to the خَبَر when لَيْسَ is added? — A: One of two things: it takes a fatḥa, or the بَاء is attached to it and it takes a kasra instead.
[00:08:00] Q: Is there a difference between the two? — A: No difference in meaning; the Qur'ān uses both, as in لَسْتَ مُؤْمِنًا with the fatḥa and أَلَيْسَ اللَّهُ بِكَافٍ عَبْدَهُ with the بَاء.

[00:14:07] Q: Why do some plurals carry a wāw and others do not? — A: That is جَمْع مُذَكَّر سَالِم, which marks case with a letter rather than a vowel: a wāw where a ḍamma would be, a yāʾ where a fatḥa or kasra would be.
[00:29:00] Q: Does اسْم التَّفْضِيل ever take tanwīn? — A: Never. It is غَيْر مُنْصَرِف, a category of words that take neither kasra nor tanwīn.
[00:37:00] Q: Do the ordinal numbers have a feminine version? — A: Yes, each has one.
[00:34:00] Q: Is أَكْبَر here the biggest or bigger? — A: Bigger, by comparison — the superlative sense would require it to be مُضَاف rather than followed by مِن.
[00:28:03] Q: Where does أَفْصَح occur in the Qur'ān? — A: In Mūsā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَام's words about his brother: وَأَخِي هَارُونُ هُوَ أَفْصَحُ مِنِّي لِسَانًا.

quiz.q: What are the two ways the خَبَر of لَيْسَ can appear?
options: With a ḍamma, or with أل
With a fatḥa, or preceded by the بَاء and so taking a kasra
With a kasra, or in the plural
quiz.a: Both are used with no change in meaning — لَسْتَ مُؤْمِنًا against لَسْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِمُسَيْطِرٍ.

quiz.q: Why does مُسَيْطِر carry a kasra in لَسْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِمُسَيْطِرٍ?
options: Because لَيْسَ always gives a kasra
Because the بَاء is a حَرْف الجَرّ
Because it is a مُضَاف إِلَيْهِ
Because it is جَمْع مُذَكَّر سَالِم
quiz.a: The بَاء attached to the خَبَر is a حَرْف الجَرّ, and those put the following word in the genitive.

quiz.q: In numbers 11 to 20, what case and number does the مَعْدُود take?
quiz.a: The first rule the teacher put on the board: from 11 to 20 the counted noun is always singular and always carries a fatḥa.

quiz.q: How is thirteen female students expressed?
quiz.a: From 13 to 19 the first part takes the opposite gender to the مَعْدُود and عَشْرَة takes the same gender, so a feminine مَعْدُود gives ثَلَاثَ عَشْرَةَ.

quiz.q: How do 11 and 12 differ from 13 to 19?
options: Their number matches the gender of the مَعْدُود throughout, rather than splitting
They take a kasra instead of a fatḥa
They do not change for gender at all
quiz.a: For 11 and 12 the whole عَدَد agrees in gender with the مَعْدُود; the split only begins at 13.

quiz.q: On which pattern is اسْم التَّفْضِيل built?
quiz.a: جَمِيل becomes أَجْمَل, وَاسِع becomes أَوْسَع, فَصِيح becomes أَفْصَح — all on أَفْعَل.

quiz.q: What makes أَطْوَل mean the tallest rather than taller?
options: Making it مُضَاف to the following noun
quiz.a: أَطْوَلُ مِنْهُ is taller than him; أَطْوَلُ طَالِبٍ فِي الْفَصْلِ, as a مُضَاف, is the tallest student in the class.

quiz.q: If someone asks أَلَسْتُ أَحْسَنَ طَالِبٍ فِي الْفَصْلِ and you want to agree that he is the best, what do you answer?
quiz.a: نَعَمْ would confirm the negative — yes, you are not. بَلَى negates the negation and so affirms the statement, the sense it carries in بَلَىٰ وَهُوَ الْخَلَّاقُ الْعَلِيمُ.

quiz.q: In خَالِدُ بْنُ الْوَلِيدِ, why does الْوَلِيد carry a kasra?
options: Because it is a proper noun
Because ابْن is مُضَاف to it
Because it follows a حَرْف الجَرّ
quiz.a: ابْن takes its own vowel from the word before it as its صِفَة, but it is مُضَاف to the name after it, which therefore takes the kasra.

options: My full blood brother, as opposed to the loose use of أَخِي
quiz.a: The teacher noted that Arabs call almost anyone أَخِي, so شَقِيق is added to make the literal relation explicit.

quran_examples.translation: You are not over them a controller.
quran_examples.note: The teacher's first example of the خَبَر of لَيْسَ taking the بَاء, which puts مُصَيْطِر into the genitive.

quran_examples.arabic: وَلَا تَقُولُوا لِمَنْ أَلْقَىٰ إِلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامَ لَسْتَ مُؤْمِنًا
quran_examples.transliteration: wa-lā taqūlū li-man alqā ilaykumu al-salāma lasta muʾminā
quran_examples.translation: And do not say to one who gives you a greeting of peace: You are not a believer.
quran_examples.note: The contrasting case, where the خَبَر مُؤْمِنًا simply takes a fatḥa with no بَاء — the teacher's proof that both constructions are correct.

quran_examples.translation: Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?
quran_examples.note: Offered in class as another instance of the بَاء on the خَبَر, here inside a negative question.

quran_examples.arabic: وَإِذْ أَخَذَ رَبُّكَ مِن بَنِي آدَمَ مِن ظُهُورِهِمْ ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ وَأَشْهَدَهُمْ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ أَلَسْتُ بِرَبِّكُمْ ۖ قَالُوا بَلَىٰ
quran_examples.transliteration: wa-idh akhadha rabbuka min banī ādama min ẓuhūrihim dhurriyyatahum wa-ashhadahum ʿalā anfusihim a-lastu bi-rabbikum, qālū balā
quran_examples.translation: And when your Lord took from the children of Ādam, from their loins, their descendants and made them testify concerning themselves: Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes, we have testified.
quran_examples.note: A student's answer, and it carries both points of the lesson at once: أَلَسْتُ بِرَبِّكُمْ with the بَاء, answered by بَلَى rather than نَعَمْ.

quran_examples.arabic: لَيْسُوا سَوَاءً ۗ مِّنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ أُمَّةٌ قَائِمَةٌ يَتْلُونَ آيَاتِ اللَّهِ آنَاءَ اللَّيْلِ وَهُمْ يَسْجُدُونَ
quran_examples.transliteration: laysū sawāʾan, min ahli al-kitābi ummatun qāʾimatun yatlūna āyāti llāhi ānāʾa al-layli wa-hum yasjudūn
quran_examples.translation: They are not all alike. Among the People of the Scripture is a community standing in obedience, reciting the verses of Allah during the night and prostrating.
quran_examples.note: The example the class gave for لَيْسُوا, the third-person masculine plural of لَيْسَ, with the teacher noting it shows Allah عَزَّ وَجَلَّ does not generalise about a whole group.

quran_examples.arabic: أَوَلَيْسَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ بِقَادِرٍ عَلَىٰ أَن يَخْلُقَ مِثْلَهُم ۚ بَلَىٰ وَهُوَ الْخَلَّاقُ الْعَلِيمُ
quran_examples.transliteration: a-wa-laysa alladhī khalaqa al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍa bi-qādirin ʿalā an yakhluqa mithlahum, balā wa-huwa al-khallāqu al-ʿalīm
quran_examples.translation: Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them? Yes indeed — and He is the Knowing Creator.
quran_examples.note: The teacher's example for بَلَى answering a negative question in the affirmative, and it also shows the بَاء on the خَبَر of لَيْسَ.

quran_examples.arabic: وَأَخِي هَارُونُ هُوَ أَفْصَحُ مِنِّي لِسَانًا
quran_examples.transliteration: wa-akhī hārūnu huwa afṣaḥu minnī lisānā
quran_examples.translation: And my brother Hārūn is more eloquent than me in speech.
quran_examples.note: A student's answer for أَفْصَح, and a clean example of اسْم التَّفْضِيل followed by مِن giving the comparative sense.
